problem.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem.prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. Return the answer in any order. The algorithm must be better than O(N log N), where N is the array length.
requirements: Return exactly k distinct elements with the highest frequencies.
Return elements in any order; no sorting of the output is required.
Support negative integers and repeated values.
Do not mutate the input array.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ U, where U is the number of unique elements.
The answer set is guaranteed to be unique.

spark.summary: Find the k most frequent integers without sorting all elements. Count occurrences, group values by frequency, and scan buckets from highest to lowest.
spark.keyTakeaway: Frequency cannot exceed the input length. Use that bounded range as bucket indices to select the top k in O(N) expected time and O(N) auxiliary space.

problem.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem.prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. Return the answer in any order. The algorithm must be better than O(N log N), where N is the array length.
problem.scopeNote: A finite integer array and a local function. No gateways, databases, availability SLOs, or distributed partitions.
requirements: Return exactly k distinct elements with the highest frequencies.
Return elements in any order; no sorting of the output is required.
Support negative integers and repeated values.
Do not mutate the input array.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ U, where U is the number of unique elements.
The answer set is guaranteed to be unique.
problem.assumptions: Inputs satisfy the stated constraints. The reference function does not perform runtime validation. The playground validates custom input before execution.

concept.whyItMatters: This problem tests frequency counting, selection instead of full sorting, and the ability to exploit a bounded integer range.

terms.name: U
terms.definition: Number of unique input values; U ≤ N.

terms.name: Frequency bucket
terms.definition: A collection of values with the same occurrence count.

keyPoints: Count values with a hash map.
Frequency, not the input value, is the bucket index.
Every unique value belongs to exactly one bucket.
Visit frequency buckets in descending order.
Stop immediately after collecting k values.
commonMistakes: Sorting all unique values and claiming a general linear-time bound.
Using input values as bucket indices; negative values make this unsuitable.
Allocating shared bucket arrays with Array(N + 1).fill([]).
Appending an entire bucket when only a few more values are needed.
Assuming a size-k heap eliminates the O(U) exact frequency map.
Confusing a unique answer set with a required output order.

sections.title: Clarify what counts.
sections.body: We need the most frequent values, not the largest values. A full sort is unnecessary because only k winners matter.
sections.interviewQuote: I’ll count occurrences first. Since every frequency is between 1 and N, I can group values by frequency and scan downward without comparison sorting.
sections.note: The unique-answer guarantee means there is no unresolved tie across the kth-place boundary. Ties inside the selected set are fine; output order is arbitrary.

sections.title: Turn counts into indices.
sections.body: A frequency map answers how often each value appears. An array of N + 1 buckets reverses that relationship: bucket[f] contains the values that appear f times.
invariants: After counting, the sum of all frequencies equals N.
Every distinct value appears in exactly one frequency bucket.
Before visiting bucket f, all buckets with greater frequencies have been processed.
The result contains only distinct values and never exceeds k entries.
sections.note: Bucket traversal and pointer-free array operations are linear. The overall O(N) bound assumes average constant-time hash map access; it is not a language-level worst-case guarantee for Map.

sections.title: Watch the buckets fill.
sections.body: Count each number, place it in its frequency bucket, and collect from the largest frequency downward. The playground displays only nonempty buckets.
sections.hint: Custom input must also satisfy the unique-answer guarantee. A tie across the selection boundary is rejected rather than silently adding a tie-breaking rule.

sections.title: Three passes. One early return.
sections.body: Create each populated bucket separately. Append values one at a time so we return exactly k entries without large spread operations or a final slice.

steps.title: Count occurrences.
steps.detail: Build Map<number, number> in a single pass over nums.

steps.title: Group by frequency.
steps.detail: Allocate N + 1 bucket slots and create lists only for frequencies that occur.

steps.title: Collect from highest to lowest.
steps.detail: Visit each bucket in descending frequency order. Return as soon as result.length equals k.

sections.note: The final return satisfies TypeScript’s control-flow requirements. With valid k, the function returns from inside the bucket traversal.

sections.title: Explain why it works.
sections.body: Descending bucket traversal visits values in nonincreasing frequency order. Therefore, the first k collected values form the required top-k set.
sections.testingNote: Compare results as sets, and separately assert result.length === k. Array order is not part of the contract.

sections.title: Know the alternatives.
sections.body: Bucket selection is a strong fit for this finite-array problem. Compare alternatives using N for total elements and U for unique values—not interchangeable symbols.

alternatives.name: Sort unique values
alternatives.tradeOff: Simple, but can reach O(N log N) when U scales with N.

alternatives.name: Size-k min-heap
alternatives.tradeOff: Compact selection structure, but not uniformly better than O(N log N) when k and U scale with N.

alternatives.name: Quickselect on counts
alternatives.time: O(N + U) expected; O(N + U²) worst case
alternatives.tradeOff: Avoids N bucket slots but introduces partition logic and pivot-dependent worst cases.

alternatives.name: Frequency buckets
alternatives.tradeOff: Direct selection using the frequency bound; may allocate more slots than needed when U is small.

followUps.question: What if memory is tighter?
followUps.answer: Quickselect uses O(U) auxiliary storage for counts and unique values. A size-k heap also requires the O(U) exact count map, even though its selection structure is only O(k).

followUps.question: What if input arrives as a stream?
followUps.answer: Clarify whether counts are over all history or a finite window, and whether approximate results are allowed. A size-k heap alone does not provide bounded-memory exact counting for unbounded unique keys. Streaming heavy-hitter methods are a different problem.

followUps.question: What if the answer is not guaranteed to be unique?
followUps.answer: Clarify whether any valid top-k set is acceptable or whether a secondary rule, such as smaller value first, is required. The original problem needs no extra tie-breaking rule.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is an array of N + 1 frequency buckets sufficient?

options.text: Every input value must be between 0 and N.
An element can occur at most N times.
There are always exactly N unique elements.

knowledgeCheck.correctExplanation: Correct. Frequency is bounded by the input length, even when the input values are negative or much larger than N.
knowledgeCheck.incorrectExplanation: The bucket index is an occurrence count, not an input value. No value can occur more than N times.

questions.prompt: When solving "Top K Frequent Elements", which failure mode is most critical to address under peak load?

options.text: Bounding queues, isolating hot keys, and enforcing explicit timeouts/idempotency.
options.explanation: Correct — protecting the critical path prevents cascading collapse under peak load.

options.text: Removing all timeouts and retries so requests wait indefinitely.
options.explanation: Unbounded waits exhaust worker threads and connection pools, causing total outages.

options.text: Skipping capacity estimation and sizing all tiers identically.
options.explanation: Read/write asymmetry and bottleneck sizing drive the architecture.
